Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
Hay-Zama Aerial Wood Bison Survey (2018) 
 
 
Introduction 
The Hay-Zama wood bison herd (Bison bison athabascae) was created by re-introducing wood bison as part of the 
Nation Wood Bison Recovery Plan, which calls for establishing a herd of free -ranging, self-sustaining and disease-
free wood bison in each of the provinces and territories in Western Canada. The Hay -Zama herd is managed by a 
controlled hunting season to consist of between 400 to 600 animals. The hunt is important to limit bison spreading 
towards Highway 35 and potential contact with diseased bison that currently exist to the east in Caribou Mountains 
Wildland Provincial Park and Wood Buffalo National park. 
For more information about management of the Hay-Zama Wood Bison herd and on issues of diseased bison in 
Alberta, please see:  
 Wood Bison Hunt - Hay-Zama 
 Wood Bison Disease Management  
A minimum total count is conducted annual in late February or March for determine size of this herd. All bison 
found are classified as to adult or juvenile and their locations plotted. 
 
Survey Method 
The survey was conducted by flying transects orientated west-east and spaced one degree of latitude apart 
(roughly one statue mile). The crew consisted of 2 observers in a Bell Jet Ranger equipped with bubble windows in 
the rear. Survey speed was approximately 90 to 110 km per hour on line.  Locations of bison tracks were plotted 
and the crew would follow fresh tracks to find bison. All groups were photographed to confirm total counts and 
classification of calves, which can be difficult in the air if bison become disturbed by the presence of the helicopter. 
Calves were classified based on relatively small size and shorter nasal bridge. Locations of other wildlife and of 
feral horses were also recorded. 
 
Results and Discussion 
3293 km of transects were surveyed from Feb. 27 to March 2, 2018 inclusively and 316 bison were seen in 7 
different groups. The percentage of calves was 17%, higher than the 5-year running average. Given the 
management objective of 400-600 bison, a suspension of the harvest for 2018-19 is recommended.
